thread.title: 1.4 million impacted by Central Ohio Primary Care Physicians data breach - NewsBreak
thread.title_full: 1.4 million impacted by Central Ohio Primary Care Physicians data breach - NewsBreak

author: Isabel Cleary
title: 1.4 million impacted by Central Ohio Primary Care Physicians data breach - NewsBreak
text:
By Isabel Cleary ,
11 hours ago
COLUMBUS, Ohio (WCMH) -- Central Ohio Primary Care Physicians was breached in August and is getting ready to notify more than one million people who are impacted, NBC4 has confirmed.
COPC has confirmed to NBC4 that 1.4 million people were impacted in this breach.
COPC is a physician-founded and led primary care group with more than 80 locations around central Ohio. It is one of the largest physician-owned primary care groups in the United States.
The organization shared that it had been a target of "vishing," or voice phishing, which attempted to solicit a financial response. Through the attack, a ransomware group was able to gain unauthorized access to protected patient information.
Sources told NBC4 the ransomware group "Chaos" hacked COPC and stole personal information. COPC confirmed that the information includes names, addresses, Social Security numbers, financial information and limited health-related patient data.
"Name, Social Security number and address combined," cybersecurity expert Shawn Waldman said. "I mean, those three are bad enough, but combined with things like patient ID and financial information, I mean, just about anything that was in that patient's file equals just about anything. So we're talking credit cards can be opened, to bank accounts. This is a severe compromise of personal, identifiable information or patient health information that can be really disastrous."
Those impacted will receive notices in the mail. COPC said the incident is contained and patients are safe to log into MyChart.
The investigation is ongoing; however, COPC says it is not aware of any misuse of personal information for identity theft or fraud stemming from the incident.
“We take this matter seriously and are implementing enhanced security protocols to further protect our systems, our team members and everyone who trusts us with their personal information," Don Deep, CEO of COPC, said in a statement. "Their peace of mind during this time is important to us as is the confidence they have in us to do all we can to support them.”
COPC will pay for credit and dark web monitoring for those impacted and will be opening a call center Thursday afternoon to answer questions. Those impacted can visit the dedicated webpage for more information.
"If you do things like freezing your credit and getting the IRS pin and some of the other stuff, now you're taking action, now you're preventing something from happening in the first place versus waiting to wake up the next morning and see that your data has been compromised and then you have to do something," Waldman said.
According to HIPPA Breach Notifications rule, covered entities have 60 days after the date of the breach was discovered to provide notification to victims. The breach was discovered on Aug. 25.
"Cyber is a cat and mouse game," Waldman said. "It's escalation. So, the threat actor does this and you respond with this. An incident happens, you learn how they got through, you bolster your responses. But then the bad guy comes up with another way to do things. Unfortunately, there is no way to stop any cyber threat from happening. The most important thing to do is the things that you and I get our and tell people to do -- get in front of it, monitor, check your, check your credit reports, make sure you're looking at your bank accounts, be as proactive as you can."
